messages.author: ebac19664dad3407
messages.subject: Modeling of multimodal data distributions
parts:
Can anyone offer advice for an analysis problem I'm working on.  I want to apply a partial-pooling approach like the radon examples in chapter 12 of ARM to analyzing a database of arsenic concentration in well-water. I have a measured arsenic concentrations in roughly 465,000 wells distrtibuted among roughly 3700 sites with the number or wells per site  ranging from 1 to roughly 2300 (the median is 82).

Right now, I'm getting started by trying a partially pooled analysis of mean arsenic and uncertainty at each site, similar to figure 12.1 in ARM. Once I'm confident this is working, I plan to build on this to add parameters that account for the effect of well depth, stratigraphic characteristics, and ultimately to consider spatial effects (e.g., draw inferences from the nearest neighbor sites).

The precision of arsenic measurements is sufficiently poor that it's reasonable for me to add 1 part per billion to every measurement (to deal with the measurements that are nominally zero parts per billion) and then take the log (base 10 to make it easier for me to interpret in terms of real units). On a log10 scale, I see a big spike at zero (about 60,000 wells) and a distinct and separate lump that looks fairly normal (corresponding to a lognormal distribution in the raw data) centered at around 2 (90,000 wells with log10(As) between 2.0 and 2.1) and nothing in the range 0.1 < x <  1.

The simple thing to do in modeling this would be to represent the data with a mixture of two normal distributions, one with a mean near zero and small variance and the other with a larger mean and variance. But a naive formulation would make the parameters of the two normal distributions non-identifiable because the distributions are invariant under swapping (mu_1, sigma_1) with (mu_2, sigma_2). And if I am doing a two-level model (a national-level (completely pooled) two-component mixture model with parameters mu_1, sigma_2, mu_2, and sigma_2, and then 3700 site-level (partially pooled) distributions with means mu_1 + delta_mu_1[i] and mu_2 + delta_mu_2[i]) there will be thousands of parameters so I have to assume that there will be a fair bit of label swapping as the MCMC does its sampling.

I would love advice about how to think about this.  Since empirically I see that the two components of my proposed mixture are well separated, I could use the empirical data to impose restrictive priors that reduce the chance of parameter swapping to low probabilities. I could also impose an ordering condition on the means. I think I wouldn't run into problems of ambiguity with ordered means because empirically the two parts of the distribution are so cleanly separated.

But I'm a newbie at this kind of analysis and would appreciate any advice on whether there's a better approach or if there are pitfalls I should watch out for beyond those mentioned in the Stan manual chapters on Mixture Models and Label Switching.

What I'm most interested in as an output is predictions of arsenic for new wells at the sites in my database, not the values of parameters for their own sake, so marginalizing out inconvenient parameters would be acceptable where that helps.

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: Modeling of multimodal data distributions
parts:
Any chance that the spike around zero is caused by censoring? In other words, is it possible that under a certain threshold for the true concentration, the measured concentrations turn out as zero? Not an uncommon phenomenon, which can be easily modeled by either:

1) integrating out the censored observations, using cumulative distribution functions, or
2) sampling the values under the threshold value (i.e. specifying them as parameters bounded between zero and the detection threshold).

Depending on the data and model, 1) or 2) may be more efficient. In one of my own applications I found the second to be more efficient, although I'm not quite sure why. Anyway, this approach doesn't require mixture distributions (if it applies to your problem).

Luc

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modeling of multimodal data distributions
parts: Hey—arsenic, that’s one of my topics!  Quick answer is that you can avoid the aliasing problem by restricting mu_1 to be less than mu_2.  You also want to put informative priors on the variance parameters, otherwise the fit can blow up with variance estimates near 0.
